newsitem.title: USA: G7 leaders call on IMF to plan increase in resources.
newsitem.headline: G7 leaders call on IMF to plan increase in resources.

text.p: Leaders of the Group of Seven industrial nations called on the International Monetary Fund on Saturday to work out a plan to increase its financial resources before September's IMF/World Bank annual meeting.

In a draft of a statement to be issued later in the day, they also said they wanted agreement on changing the IMF's constitution to allow it to go ahead with a selective issue of its articial currency, Special Drawing Rights (SDR).
"We ask the IMF board to work toward completing the ... review of quotas by the time of the Hong Kong World Bank/IMF meetings in September," the draft statement said.

Quotas are contributions from member countries which provide the IMF with its capital which currently stands at 145.3 billion SDRs ($202 billion). The IMF board is considering an increase of between 35 and 60 percent in its current resources.

The board is also discussing a selective allocation of SDRs mainly aimed at about 40 member nations which do not have any holdings of the IMF currency in their reserves. The size of the issue was expected to be between 20 and 22.4 billion SDRs ($27.8 billion and $31.1 billion).
The G7 comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. Russian President Boris Yeltsin has joined their leaders at the Denver "Summit of the Eight" ending on Sunday.
The leaders said they wanted further changes to the IMF constitution to give the fund a mandate to promote the free flow of capital worldwide.
They called for substantial agreement on that change by the time of the Hong Kong meeting.
Some developing countries are uneasy about the risks posed by throwing open their economies to the mercy of often fickle foreign capital flows.

G7 leaders also pledged to provide the IMF's Enhanced Structural Adjustment facility and the World Bank's Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) with sufficient resources to carry on their activities.

The ESAF provides cheap loans to poor countries carrying out wrenching changes to their economies. The MIGA guarantees investments in developing countries against expropriation and sudden policy changes by governments.
Leaders said a well-funded ESAF was needed "to maintain a full role for the IMF in promoting growth and development in the poorest countries".

"It is incumbent on us to help ensure that the international financial institutions have the multilateral support and financial resources needed to succeed with their ambitious and important reforms," the statement said.

In an apparent criticism of the United States, which is running behind on contributions to the World Bank, it called on all G7 countries to meet financial commitments in full to allow international institutions to help developing countries.
The G7 welcomed the World Bank's plans to support private sector infrastructure investment in developing countries.
